Maxillary nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion
At a glance

The maxillary nerve (V2) is the second division of the trigeminal nerve; this lesson covers its course, its branches, and the pterygopalatine ganglion suspended from it.

Course of the maxillary nerve

Source: PDF page 67

The maxillary nerve is the second division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve, and it passes in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.

To reach its destination in the face it passes through four openings: two foramina and two fissures.

  1. Foramen rotundum

    The nerve leaves the cranial cavity and enters the pterygopalatine fossa.

  2. Pterygomaxillary fissure

    The nerve enters the anterior part of the infratemporal fossa.

  3. Inferior orbital fissure

    The nerve enters the orbit, where it becomes the infraorbital nerve. It passes through the infra-orbital groove and the infra-orbital canal.

  4. Infraorbital foramen

    The nerve leaves the orbit and reaches the face as the infraorbital nerve.

Branches of the maxillary nerve

Source: PDF page 67
  1. Meningeal branch: arises in the cranial cavity and supplies the dura mater.
  2. Ganglionic branches: suspend the pterygopalatine ganglion.
  3. Zygomatic nerve: arises in the infratemporal fossa and enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure. It divides into the zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal branches.
  4. Posterior superior alveolar nerve.
  5. Infraorbital nerve: gives the middle and anterior superior alveolar nerves. It then emerges from the infraorbital foramen and divides into palpebral, nasal and labial branches.

The pterygopalatine ganglion and its roots

Source: PDF page 67
High-yield

The pterygopalatine ganglion is the largest parasympathetic ganglion of the head and neck. It lies in the pterygopalatine fossa, suspended from the maxillary nerve.

The three roots

RootSourceHow it reaches the ganglion
SensoryTwo ganglionic branches from the maxillary nerveDirectly, as the ganglionic branches
SympatheticPlexus around the internal carotid arteryThrough the deep petrosal nerve
ParasympatheticPreganglionic fibers from the superior salivary nucleusPass with the facial nerve, then the greater petrosal nerve, which unites with the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic root) to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve). The Vidian nerve passes through the pterygoid canal to end in the ganglion.

Branches of the pterygopalatine ganglion

Source: PDF page 68
Lacrimal gland
Postganglionic parasympathetic fibers (route below)
Orbital branches
Enter the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure
Greater and lesser palatine
Supply the palate and the nasal cavity

Route of the fibers to the lacrimal gland

Pterygopalatine ganglion
Zygomatic nerve
Zygomatico-temporal nerve
Lacrimal nerve
Lacrimal gland

The zygomatico-temporal nerve gives a twig to the lacrimal nerve, and the lacrimal nerve carries the fibers to the gland.

Check yourself

Name the four openings the maxillary nerve passes through, in order.

Foramen rotundum, pterygomaxillary fissure, inferior orbital fissure, and infraorbital foramen.

Which two nerves unite to form the nerve of the pterygoid canal (Vidian nerve)?

The greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic root).

How do postganglionic parasympathetic fibers reach the lacrimal gland?

They pass with the zygomatic nerve, then the zygomatico-temporal nerve, which gives a twig to the lacrimal nerve; the lacrimal nerve carries them to the gland.

Key Points / Quick Review

Maxillary nerve (V2)

  • Second division of the trigeminal nerve; passes in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.
  • Four openings: foramen rotundum, pterygomaxillary fissure, inferior orbital fissure, infraorbital foramen.
  • Becomes the infraorbital nerve in the orbit and reaches the face through the infraorbital foramen.

Branches of V2

  • Meningeal, ganglionic, zygomatic, posterior superior alveolar, infraorbital.
  • Zygomatic nerve divides into zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal branches.
  • Infraorbital nerve gives middle and anterior superior alveolar nerves, then palpebral, nasal and labial branches.

Pterygopalatine ganglion

  • Largest parasympathetic ganglion of the head and neck, in the pterygopalatine fossa.
  • Roots: sensory (ganglionic branches), sympathetic (deep petrosal nerve), parasympathetic (greater petrosal nerve, then Vidian nerve).
  • Branches: fibers to the lacrimal gland, orbital branches, greater and lesser palatine nerves.
